verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse.sanskrit: ध्यायतो विषयान्पुंसः सङ्गस्तेषूपजायते । सङ्गात् संजायते कामः कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते ॥
verse.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.
verse.why: Steadiness is built by guarding attention; anger starts with what you dwell on.

prasang.title: The person of steady wisdom
prasang.summary: Arjuna asks how a steady person speaks, sits and walks. Krishna describes someone content within, unshaken by sorrow, master of the senses, and traces how dwelling on things leads to anger and ruin.
prasang.lesson: Steadiness is built by guarding attention; anger starts with what you dwell on.

verse.meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna what a steady mind looks like, and Krishna tells him that steadiness is built by guarding attention. When you dwell on objects, attachment is born. That attachment turns into wanting, and when that wanting is blocked, it turns into anger.
verse.for_you: You are trying to hold the outcome of your work and care steady so you can rest. But the mind cannot hold the future.
verse.try_today: Notice where your attention has settled today.
verse.scene_line: You are sitting in the waiting room of your own life.
asks: How do I stop my mind from running ahead?

verse.line: Not begging for gain, not grieving loss: a steady mind stays cool and full.
verse.translation: He does not pray for gain, nor grieve over loss. The steady one's cool mind is filled as if with nectar.

prasang.title: The calm of the wise

prasang.lesson: Calm isn't found by chasing it or changing places; it is how you hold ordinary life.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: On wealth
prasang.summary: A wry look at money: how the world flatters the rich and forgets the broke, wealth's three destinies, and how distance and neglect ruin what we value. It closes with advice to the chataka bird not to plead before every cloud.
prasang.lesson: Money changes how others see you, not who you are. Give it, enjoy it, or lose it.

story.title: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
story.story_hook: One spring morning, a king out for a walk overheard a song that he could not stop thinking about.
story.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to the day's work, he decides not to run away: he gets up and does his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutches.
story.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

anchor.speaker: Janaka
anchor.setting: King Janaka, alone on his palace roof after overhearing wandering sages, rethinks his life.
anchor.sanskrit: संपदश्च विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेच्चित्तेन संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा हन्त मन्ये महापदः ॥ आपदोऽपि विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेन्मनसि संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा मन्ये मनसि संपदः ॥
anchor.line: Good fortune the mind clutches becomes trouble. Trouble the mind accepts becomes a kind of fortune.
anchor.translation: All those dazzling fortunes, if the mind clings to them, are really great calamities in grand disguise. And all those varied misfortunes, if the mind accepts them, are really fortunes.
anchor.why: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.
anchor.misuse: Accepting a hardship doesn't mean not fixing what can be fixed.

prasang.title: Two old friends meet again and admit they never found peace
prasang.summary: Bhasa and Vilasa grow up inseparable in a forest hermitage. After their fathers die they drift apart and spend long lonely years in hard austerities. When they meet again as old men, one asks if the other is well; he answers honestly that there is no wellness while the mind keeps spinning through endless tasks and worries.
prasang.story_hook: They had been inseparable as boys, and when they met again they were old men with nothing to show.
prasang.lesson: Years of hard effort without inner understanding can leave you exactly where you started.

verse.meaning: Two old friends, Bhasa and Vilasa, meet again after decades apart. Bhasa asks if Vilasa is well. Vilasa admits he is not. He says his mind is caught on endless lists of what he has done, what he is doing, and what he must still do. It is tangled in a net of reckonings, and because of this, it faints. The verse shows that years of hard work, without inner understanding, can leave you exactly where you started. It is not the work itself that exhausts you.
verse.for_you: You are living inside that endless list. The work, the care, the worry about how things will turn out. It is a heavy weight, and you have carried it for a long time. The mind does not get a moment's rest because it is trying to hold everything at once.
verse.try_today: Notice the moment you add the next thing to your list. Just see it there.
verse.scene_line: You are the old man, caught in a net of reckonings, admitting you have never found peace.

verse.line: Stay anchored within while you do all your outer work, and you won't burn out.
verse.translation: Staying turned inward while doing all the outer work that comes to you, you will never grow weary, and you will be free of the sense of being the doer.
verse.why: Work fully, enjoy fully, let go fully; anchored inside, you can do it all without burning out.

prasang.title: Shiva's three vows: be a great doer, enjoyer and letter-go
prasang.summary: Vasishtha gives Rama three vows that Shiva once gave his devotee Bhringi: be a great doer, a great enjoyer, and a great renouncer. A great doer acts fully and on time without clinging; a great enjoyer takes in joys and sorrows evenly, like the ocean takes in rivers; a great renouncer lets go inside. Live this way and work won't wear you out.
prasang.lesson: Work fully, enjoy fully, let go fully; anchored inside, you can do it all without burning out.

verse.meaning: Vasishtha finishes his teaching to Rama, who is preparing to return to the world after three years of silence. Vasishtha gives him three vows that Shiva once gave his devotee Bhringi. The first is to be a great doer, acting fully and on time without clinging to results. The second is to be a great enjoyer, taking in joys and sorrows evenly like the ocean takes in rivers. The third is to be a great renouncer, letting go inside.
verse.for_you: You move from one task to the next, caught in the loop of what must be done. The mind races ahead to how things will turn out, and that is what leaves you burned out. Stay anchored within while you do your outer work.
verse.try_today: Notice the difference between finishing a task and letting go of the result.
verse.scene_line: You are a great doer, acting fully, letting the result go.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Arjuna asks which devotee is best; Krishna offers a ladder of practices.
verse.line: Practice is good, understanding better, meditation better still. But letting go of results brings peace at once.
verse.translation: Knowledge is better than mere practice; meditation is better than knowledge; giving up the fruit of action is better than meditation. From that renunciation, peace follows immediately.
verse.why: If the ideal is too hard, take the next step down, and keep going.
verse.misuse: Not 'stop caring how things turn out'. Peace comes from releasing the grip, not from indifference.

prasang.title: Form or formless: which devotee is best, and the ways to reach him

prasang.lesson: If the ideal is too hard, take the next step down, and keep going.

verse.meaning: Krishna is answering Arjuna's question about the best way to reach God. Arjuna wants a clear path. Krishna offers a ladder of practices, from devotion to meditation to action. But he says the final step is letting go of results. The verse says that if you let go of the fruit of your action, peace comes immediately. You do not have to be perfect. You just have to release your grip on how things turn out.
verse.for_you: The work for your parents and your job is heavy. You are trying to make sure the outcome is right before you rest. That grip is what is exhausting you. Let the outcome be what it is. Your part is to act steadily. That balance is enough.
verse.try_today: Do one task for your parents or work without checking how it turns out.
verse.scene_line: You stand at the bottom of the ladder, holding the outcome in your hands.
asks: How do I let go of the outcome without stopping caring?
What does steady action look like when I am this tired?

verse.line: Do what comes to you to do, then let it go and live at ease.
verse.translation: Seeing truly that nothing done is ever really done by me, I do whatever comes to be done and live happily.
verse.why: Happiness can be simple: do what comes, stop both grabbing and renouncing.

prasang.title: Janaka's songs of simple happiness

prasang.lesson: Happiness can be simple: do what comes, stop both grabbing and renouncing.

verse.meaning: Janaka tells Ashtavakra that he sees no real doer behind any action, so he simply does what comes and lives happily. The point is that happiness can be simple: do what comes, stop both grabbing and renouncing.
verse.for_you: The work and the care will not turn out the way you want them to. The tiredness is not the illness or the deadline, it is the waiting for a finish line that never arrives. The next move is to do the next thing and let it go.
verse.try_today: Do the next task, then stop thinking about the outcome.

story.summary: Hanuman searches Lanka all night without finding Sita. He is close to despair, weighing what failure will mean for everyone, then tells himself that refusing to lose heart is the root of success, and searches again.
story.lesson: When you have looked everywhere, look again; giving up costs too much.

anchor.line: Giving up costs too much. Whoever keeps going finds good things again.

verse.line: The body comes and goes; what you truly are does not. Why grieve so?

verse.line: Teach me how to keep working in the world without the work filling me with sorrow.
verse.translation: Tell me the skill by which sorrow doesn't come to me while I go about my work, or else tell me the best way of dealing with life itself.

prasang.title: Rama asks how to live in the world without being crushed by it
prasang.summary: After his lament Rama turns to questions. How did King Janaka and others stay free while running kingdoms? How can a person work in the world untouched, like water on a lotus leaf? He asks for one practical skill that lets him work without sorrow.
prasang.story_hook: Having said what was wrong, Rama finally asked the question that matters: how do the wise do it?
prasang.lesson: The real question isn't whether to quit life, but how to live it without being swallowed.

verse.meaning: Rama has been asking how to be free while living in the world. He has seen that the body comes and goes, but what truly is does not. Now he asks for a practical skill. He wants to know how to go about his work without sorrow filling him. He is not asking to leave his duties. He is asking how to do what must be done without being swallowed by the weight of it. The question is not whether to act, but how to act without the result becoming a burden.
verse.for_you: You are working and caring for your parents. You feel burned out and running on empty. You are anxious about how things will turn out. You want to do the work, but the work itself is filling you with sorrow. Rama's question is your question.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how the wise live and work.
verse.sanskrit: यदृच्छालाभसन्तुष्टो द्वन्द्वातीतो विमत्सरः । समः सिद्धावसिद्धौ च कृत्वापि न निबध्यते ॥
verse.line: Content with what comes, beyond envy, steady in success and failure, you stay free even while working.
verse.translation: Content with whatever comes unasked, beyond the pairs of opposites, free from envy, the same in success and failure, even when acting he is not bound.
verse.why: Contentment and freedom from envy let you work without being bound.

prasang.title: How the great yogis live
prasang.summary: The wise act without selfish motive, content and dependent on nothing, free from envy, steady in success and failure.
prasang.lesson: Contentment and freedom from envy let you work without being bound.

verse.meaning: Krishna is telling Arjuna how the wise live. He says the great yogis are content with whatever comes without asking. They are beyond the pairs of opposites like success and failure. They are free from envy and steady in both. Even when they act, they do not become bound by the work. The idea is that contentment and freedom from envy let you work without being bound by the results.
verse.for_you: The restlessness comes from tying your rest to how things turn out at work and with your parents. The verse offers a steadiness that does not depend on the result. It is the self that stays when the role and the fear change.
verse.try_today: Notice the moment your mind asks for a result before it will settle.
verse.scene_line: You are on the edge of action, waiting for the outcome to grant you rest.

verse.line: Throne or begging bowl, gain or loss, crowd or solitude: a steady person stays the same.
verse.translation: For the yogi of steady nature there is no difference between ruling a kingdom and living on alms, gain and loss, the crowd and the forest.

verse.why: Calm isn't found by chasing it or changing places; it is how you hold ordinary life.

prasang.title: The calm of the wise
prasang.summary: In a hundred verses Ashtavakra paints the inner peace of the wise: calm while busy, unmoved by gain or loss, praise or blame, at ease whether in the city or the forest. The restless, by contrast, chase peace and never find it.
prasang.lesson: Calm isn't found by chasing it or changing places; it is how you hold ordinary life.

verse.meaning: In the final verses of his teaching, Ashtavakra stands before Janaka. He has spent the chapter describing a mind that does not chase after comfort or run from discomfort. Here he says that for someone whose nature is steady, there is no difference between ruling a kingdom and living on alms, between gain and loss, the crowd and the forest. The verse proposes that calm is not a place you go or a feeling you chase. It is the quality of how you hold whatever is already in your hand.
verse.for_you: You are holding the weight of your parents and your work, waiting for the outcome to give you permission to rest. The verse says that calm is not a reward you earn after the work is done.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment when the outcome is out of your hands, and let your body rest in that fact.

verse.line: Yoga is skill in action: doing the work well, without being bound by it.
verse.translation: One joined to this understanding casts off both good and bad results here. So devote yourself to yoga; yoga is skill in action.
verse.why: Do the work fully; let go of owning the result.

prasang.title: The yoga of action

verse.meaning: Krishna tells Arjuna that a person joined to this understanding casts off good and bad results. It is the yoga of action. Do the work fully, but give up clinging to outcomes. Stay even in success and failure and keep a single steady purpose.
verse.for_you: You are trying to rest before the work turns out the way you need it to. The Gita calls this casting off results. Let the work be the work for today. The outcome can wait. Your part is the doing.

verse.line: Results follow effort. Call it fate if you like, but it is the same effort.
verse.translation: As the effort, so quickly comes the fruit. So there is only effort; if you want to call it fate, it is that same effort.
verse.why: Your past effort shaped today; today's effort shapes tomorrow. Don't grieve what was never in your hands.

prasang.title: Vasishtha on self-effort: fate is only your past effort
prasang.summary: Vasishtha's first teaching to Rama is a long case for self-effort. What people call fate is simply the fruit of their own past effort, and present effort can overcome it, as the stronger of two rams wins. He also says not to torment yourself over what was beyond your power, and to steer your habits gently, like raising a child.
prasang.lesson: Your past effort shaped today; today's effort shapes tomorrow. Don't grieve what was never in your hands.

verse.meaning: Vasishtha is speaking to Rama. Rama is young and feels lost, as if life is just a storm of things happening to him. Vasishtha tells him that what people call fate is only the result of what they have already done. Your past effort built the world you are in right now. Your present effort is what builds the one you will enter next. The idea is simple. You do not control the fruit that falls today. You only control the effort you put in today. The past is already written.
verse.for_you: Vasishtha tells Rama that the past is already written and the future is blank. Your present effort is all you have.
verse.try_today: Notice one small action you are doing today and let the result go.
verse.scene_line: You are in your own quiet room, and the only thing in your hands is the effort you choose to make today.

story.title: Pingala's song: the night she stopped waiting
story.story_hook: Pingala sat awake listening for footsteps that never came, until she stopped listening.
story.summary: Pingala waited all night for a lover who never came. At last she saw that her peace depended on someone else's arrival, let the expectation go, and slept peacefully.
story.lesson: Letting go of an expectation can bring the sleep that waiting never will.
